images.text: Bread – most of us eat it every day, as toast at breakfast, in a sandwich at lunch, or as a perfect complement to soup or salad. Have you ever thought about the history of your daily bread? However, in ancient times, people attached great significance to bread. People have long considered bread to be sacred and to be treated with respect. For example, bread has always had religious significance in Christianity, because it is associated with Holy Communion. In Judaism, bread also has importance, as it was used in ceremonies in the ancient temple. At one time, people throughout the world thought that throwing away bread was bad luck. People superstitiously felt that anyone who threw bread away would someday end up having no food.

Many ancient beliefs and folklore have surrounded the making of bread. In some parts of Scotland, people singing while bread was baking would have bad luck. Bread being baked while the body of a family member was was lying in state waiting to be buried was also bad luck. Some people also believed that only one person should be responsible for putting bread into the oven to bake. Two people sharing the task would certainly quarrel. When the bread was baking, if you cut another loaf, it would spoil the bread that was baking. If people wanted to eat bread while they were baking a loaf, they were supposed to break the bread instead of cutting it.

In days of old, you had to take care while eating your bread as well. If a young woman took a loaf of bread and it broke apart in her hand, people believed that she would not find a husband until the following year. A loaf of bread being put onto its top crust on the dinner table would bring misfortune. Bad luck also came from cutting a loaf on both ends, or even touching it while it was being cut. And if only one slice of buttered bread was left on the plate, you couldn't take it until it was offered to you. Otherwise you would have bad luck. If an unmarried woman happened to do this, people thought that she would never marry. However, if you were offered the last piece of a loaf , you would never refuse it, as it was thought to bring not only good luck in love but money as well.

Superstitions surrounding bread were not only associated with tales of bad luck. Bread was also used in charms and spells for healing people. In the sixteenth century, people would cure a toothache by taking a small piece from a loaf of white bread, putting the sign of the cross on it, then placing it over the aching tooth. Some people believed that they could cure whooping cough by wrapping a piece of bread in cloth, burying it for three days, and then digging it up and giving it to the patient to eat.
So we see that eating bread is not as simple as it may seem. Perhaps the next time you reach for a thick slice of bread and butter you should stop and think. Is it upside down? Crumbly? Is it the last piece? Was it cut at both ends? What if you need to throw it out? Was anyone singing while baking it?

The Participle Clause: Past, Present, Being+Past Participle
Participle clauses go after a noun just like relative clauses. They add information about the noun.
You can use a past participle in the same way as passive relative clauses (using the Past tense):

We received the document sent by the publisher.
(We received the document that had been sent by the publisher.)
You can use a present participle (verb + ing) as you would an active relative clause:

The woman living next door is one of my relatives.
(The woman who is living next door is one of my relatives.)
You can use being + past participle as you would a continuous passive relative clause:
The song being sung by the singer was composed by her husband.
(The song that is being sung by the singer was composed by her husband.)

The cake being eaten at the wedding was made in Italy.
(The cake that is being eaten at the wedding was made in Italy.)

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.

I have learned English. (I learned English in the past and now I can speak English.)
He has bought a painting. (He bought the painting in the past and now he has a painting.)
It is common to use for and since when referring to time periods in the Present Perfect:

• You use FOR to talk about how long an action has been happening (a week, 2 days, five hours, six years etc.)
  • You use SINCE to talk about when the action started (2010, Monday, since she was a child)
Since the moving van pulled away that day, his life has not been the same.
Usually, when you use the Simple Past tense, the time of the finished action is clear from the context or explicitly mentioned in the sentence.

Yesterday, I went to the store.
She moved away with her parents several years ago.
It is clear when the action occurred. In this sentence we would not use the Present Perfect. (<strike>Yesterday, I have been to the store</strike>.)
